item.title: Damnatio Memoriae: How Rome Erased a Person, and Why It Never Worked
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
In the Antikensammlung in Berlin there is a circular painted wooden panel about thirty centimetres across, made in Egypt around 200 CE. It shows an imperial family: Septimius Severus with a grey beard, his wife Julia Domna, and their two sons.

One of the sons has no face. The paint has been scraped and smeared away, leaving a rough brown void where a boy's head was.

His name was Geta. In 211 CE his brother Caracalla had him killed — by most accounts in their mother's arms — and then set about removing him from the world. Someone in Egypt who owned this small domestic portrait understood what was now required of them, and took something abrasive to the face of a child they had presumably hung on a wall.

That panel is the clearest surviving image of what modern historians call damnatio memoriae: the Roman procedure for deleting a person.

What the sanction involved

It was not a single act but a bundle of measures, applied in varying combinations by decree of the Senate, usually after the target was already dead.

  • Names chiselled from inscriptions. Public monuments, dedications, milestones, building plaques — anywhere the name appeared in stone, it was cut out.
  • Images destroyed or recarved. Statues were pulled down, and marble portraits were frequently reworked into a successor's likeness. Bronze went to the furnace.
  • Coinage withdrawn. Coins bearing the condemned face were called in and melted, though hoard evidence shows this was never comprehensive.
  • Records struck. The name removed from the consular lists, from acts, from the calendar.
  • The name itself forbidden. In severe cases, descendants and relatives were barred from using it, and the birthday was declared inauspicious.

Suetonius describes the aftermath of Domitian's assassination in 96 CE: senators arriving with ladders, tearing his portraits down on the spot and smashing them, and voting to erase his inscriptions everywhere. Pliny the Younger, writing as a contemporary who was there, describes the same scene with open pleasure — the axes going into the faces, the imperial features struck off.

A note on the term

Damnatio memoriae is not a phrase Romans used. It comes from early modern legal scholarship, and it imposes a tidy unified concept on what was in practice an ad hoc, negotiated and highly variable set of penalties. Some targets got everything. Some got a few statues pulled down. Some were condemned and then quietly rehabilitated later. The Latin sources talk about specific measures, not a doctrine.

Geta, and the most thorough attempt

Caracalla's erasure of his brother is the case where the machinery ran at full power, and it is well documented precisely because it failed so visibly.

On the Arch of the Argentarii in Rome — a small monument put up by the money-changers' guild — the family is shown sacrificing. Geta's figure has been cut out of the relief, leaving an obvious rectangular gap in the composition with the surviving figures gesturing toward nothing. The dedicatory inscription has lines hacked away.

Papyri from Egypt show his name blotted out of official documents. Inscriptions across the empire have the gap. Ancient sources report that saying his name became dangerous, and Cassius Dio claims men were killed for possessing his image or mourning him.

And the result, eighteen centuries later, is that Geta is one of the better-known short-reigned emperors, chiefly because of the erasure. We can list where his name was removed, which monuments carry the gaps, and roughly how quickly the order propagated across the provinces. The deletion is a documented event with a paper trail.

The structural problem

The paradox is not subtle, and Roman elites cannot have missed it.

An erased inscription is not a blank inscription. It is an inscription with a conspicuous scar in it, cut into a legible sentence, in a public place, surrounded by intact text that explains the context. Anyone literate walking past a monument with a chiselled gap knows immediately that someone has been removed and can usually work out who from the remaining words.

Recarved statues are similar. Sculptors reworking a portrait into a successor's face left traces — proportions that no longer fit, hair recut over a different original, drill work at odd depths. Portrait specialists identify reworked heads routinely.

This is why the current scholarly consensus, argued most fully by Harriet Flower, has largely abandoned the idea that these sanctions were literal attempts at oblivion. The purpose was performance. The point of the empty space was that people should see it.

Read that way, the sanction becomes intelligible as politics. The Senate, or the successor, is making a public statement: this person's honours were illegitimate, this regime is repudiated, and the people who did the chiselling have chosen a side. A dishonoured absence is a stronger political message than a name nobody notices. The gap is the announcement.

The Egyptian versions, which are not the same

Egypt did this earlier and on a larger scale, though the motives look different.

Hatshepsut, who ruled as pharaoh in the fifteenth century BCE, had her images defaced and her name removed from monuments and king lists. The obvious reading — a resentful successor lashing out — runs into a problem: the erasures appear to have begun roughly two decades after her death, under Thutmose III, and they were selective rather than total. Immediate personal spite does not fit a twenty-year delay. Current interpretations lean toward dynastic housekeeping: securing an unambiguous male succession by removing an anomaly from the official line, without particular animus.

Akhenaten received harsher treatment. After the collapse of his religious revolution, his city was abandoned, his monuments dismantled, and his name omitted from later king lists, which skip from his predecessor to Horemheb as though the intervening decades did not occur. His temple blocks were reused as rubble fill inside later structures — which is why thousands of them survive in excellent condition, protected from weather for three thousand years by the very people trying to eliminate them.

Egyptologists recovered the Amarna period substantially from that fill. The erasure preserved the evidence.

The uncomfortable part

All of this concerns the failures, because failures are what leave traces. Which raises a question with no available answer.

We know about Geta because the erasure was clumsy, hurried, and applied across an empire too large to police. We know about Akhenaten because his stones were reused rather than ground down. Every case discussed here is a case where the procedure did not work.

There is no way to identify the cases where it did. A successful erasure produces no gap to notice, no reworked portrait to detect, no anomaly in the record — because a genuinely complete removal would also remove the evidence that anything had been removed.

What we can say is that the ancient world had both the administrative capacity and the political will to attempt this, repeatedly, over millennia. Augustus burned two thousand books of unauthorised prophecy in a single operation and we know of it only from a passing line in Suetonius.

The blank spaces we can see are the ones where somebody was in a hurry.

Questions people actually ask

What is damnatio memoriae?

The modern name for a set of Roman sanctions that removed a disgraced person from public memory: erasing their name from inscriptions, destroying or recarving their images, withdrawing their coinage, and striking them from official records.

Is 'damnatio memoriae' a Latin term the Romans used?

Not really. The phrase is a modern coinage from early modern legal scholarship. Romans described the individual measures — abolition of the name, removal of images — rather than using a single umbrella term.

Who was subjected to damnatio memoriae?

Among others Sejanus, Domitian, Commodus, Elagabalus and, most thoroughly, the emperor Geta, murdered by his brother Caracalla in 211 CE. Egyptian parallels include Hatshepsut and the Amarna pharaohs.

Did damnatio memoriae actually erase anyone?

Almost never. Erasure produces a visible blank in a public inscription, which draws attention rather than removing it. Most scholars now argue the sanction was performative — designed to be witnessed, not to succeed.

What is the Severan Tondo?

A painted wooden panel from Egypt showing Septimius Severus, Julia Domna and their two sons — with Geta's face deliberately smeared out. It is the most direct surviving image of a Roman erasure being carried out.

Sources & further reading

  • Harriet I. Flower, The Art of Forgetting: Disgrace and Oblivion in Roman Political Culture (2006) — the definitive treatment.
  • Charles W. Hedrick Jr., History and Silence: Purge and Rehabilitation of Memory in Late Antiquity (2000).
  • Suetonius, Domitian 23 — senators tearing down Domitian's images.
  • Pliny the Younger, Panegyricus 52 — a contemporary describing the same destruction with relish.
  • The Severan Tondo, Antikensammlung, Berlin — the erasure itself, preserved.
  • The Arch of the Argentarii, Rome — where Geta's figure was cut out of the relief.

item.title: The Library of Alexandria: Nobody Burned It, and That Is Worse
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
The story everyone knows goes like this. There was a library in Alexandria containing all the knowledge of the ancient world. Someone burned it. Depending on which version reaches you, the someone is Julius Caesar, a Christian mob, or a Muslim caliph. Because of that fire, civilisation lost centuries.

Essentially every element of this is wrong, and the correction is not a pedantic one. What actually happened to the Library is a more useful story, and a considerably bleaker one.

What the institution actually was

The Library was not a building full of books that people visited. It was part of the Mouseion — literally a shrine of the Muses — a royal research institution founded under the first Ptolemies in the early third century BCE.

Resident scholars were paid a salary by the crown, housed, fed, and exempted from taxes. They ate together. They had no teaching obligations. In modern terms it was a state-funded institute for advanced study, and the library was its working collection.

The acquisitions policy was famously aggressive. Ships docking at Alexandria were reportedly searched for books, which were copied — with the copy sometimes returned and the original retained. Agents were sent to buy collections abroad.

The output justified the expense. This is where Eratosthenes calculated the circumference of the Earth to within a few percent. Where Aristarchus proposed a heliocentric model eighteen centuries before Copernicus. Where the text of Homer was edited into something close to the form we read. Where Euclid probably worked. The Mouseion was, for about two centuries, the most productive concentration of scholarship on the planet.

The fires, examined individually

48 BCE, Caesar. During the Alexandrian War, Caesar's forces set fire to ships in the harbour and the fire spread ashore. That much is agreed. But the strongest account, in Cassius Dio, specifies that what burned were storehouses near the docks containing grain and books — export stock awaiting shipment, not the Mouseion's collection. The decisive evidence is Strabo, who visited Alexandria around twenty-five years later, describes the Mouseion in the present tense as a functioning institution with its covered walk and communal dining hall, and does not mention a catastrophe. He was standing there. He would have noticed.

272 CE, Aurelian. This one is under-discussed and probably mattered most. Suppressing Zenobia's revolt, Aurelian's forces devastated the Brucheion — the palace quarter that contained the Mouseion. The district was substantially destroyed and never fully recovered. If a single military event ended the institution, this is the leading candidate, and almost nobody has heard of it.

391 CE, the Serapeum. Bishop Theophilus led the destruction of the temple of Serapis, which had housed a subsidiary collection. This genuinely happened. But Ammianus Marcellinus, writing shortly before, already refers to the libraries there in the past tense — whether significant holdings remained by 391 is doubtful.

415 CE, Hypatia. Not a library event at all. Hypatia was a distinguished mathematician and philosopher murdered by a mob in a vicious episode of Alexandrian factional violence. Her death is frequently narrated as the end of the Library, which is a modern conflation. She was not a librarian, and there was no functioning Library to be the last of.

642 CE, the Caliph Omar. The famous tale — that the books were used to heat the city's bathhouses for six months, on the grounds that they either agreed with the Quran or contradicted it — first appears in sources written around six centuries after the conquest. There is no contemporary trace of it, and it is rejected by essentially all specialists. It has the shape of a polemical anecdote, and that is what it appears to be.

Why the fire story is so persistent

A fire gives you a date, a villain and a moral. Institutional decay gives you none of these. The burning of Alexandria has survived as a story for the same reason it is false: it converts a diffuse structural failure into a single dramatic act with someone to blame. Every version of the tale has been useful to someone with an argument to make about a particular group.

What actually killed it

Three unglamorous causes, all of them still recognisable.

The funding stopped. The Mouseion existed because Ptolemaic kings paid for it as a matter of dynastic prestige. When that political logic weakened, so did the institution. In 145 BCE Ptolemy VIII purged Alexandria's intellectuals in a factional dispute and scholars fled to Rhodes, Pergamon and Athens. Under Roman rule the Mouseion continued but as a shadow of the Ptolemaic operation, with appointments increasingly used as sinecures.

Papyrus does not last. This is the point most people miss and it is the central one. Papyrus in Alexandria's damp coastal climate degrades within a couple of centuries at best. A library on papyrus is not a store of books — it is a copying operation that must run continuously. Every text needs recopying every few generations or it simply ceases to exist. Stop paying the scribes and the collection dissolves on its own, silently, without anyone setting fire to anything.

Attention moved. Alexandria's monopoly ended. Pergamon built a rival library. Rome accumulated collections. Later, Constantinople became the centre of gravity for Greek texts, and it was Byzantine scribes who determined what survived to the present by choosing what to recopy.

What we actually lost

And here the myth undersells the disaster, because the losses are real — they just were not caused by a fire.

Sophocles wrote around 120 plays. We have seven. Aeschylus wrote perhaps ninety. We have seven. Of Aristotle's published works, written for a general audience and praised in antiquity for their style, we have essentially none — what survives is lecture notes. Most of Sappho is gone. Livy wrote 142 books of Roman history; 35 survive. The vast majority of Hellenistic scientific and mathematical literature is lost.

None of this happened in an afternoon. It happened because at some point, for each of those texts, the last person who was going to copy it decided not to — or died before doing it, or could not find a patron, or found the papyrus already too rotted to read.

The scale of surviving classical literature is estimated at somewhere around one percent of what once existed. That figure is not the product of arson. It is the product of a filter running for two thousand years, in which anything not actively maintained was quietly dropped.

The part that should worry you

Everything discussed elsewhere on this site — a cult whose doctrine vanished completely, an oracle of which not one authenticated line survives — is downstream of this same mechanism. The mysteries were not only kept secret. They were also, simply, not copied.

The lesson of Alexandria is not that barbarians burn books. It is that knowledge is not stored, it is maintained, and maintenance is a recurring cost that some institution has to keep choosing to pay. When the payments stop, nothing dramatic happens. The material just becomes unreadable over a period longer than anyone's attention span, and by the time the loss is visible there is nobody left who knows what was in it.

No villain is required. That is the disturbing part.

Questions people actually ask

Who burned the Library of Alexandria?

No single person or event destroyed it. The Library declined over roughly six centuries through loss of funding, political disruption, physical decay of papyrus, and the gradual end of systematic copying. Every 'the library was burned' story is either exaggerated or invented.

Did Julius Caesar burn the Library of Alexandria?

A fire during Caesar's Alexandrian campaign in 48 BCE did destroy books, but the strongest ancient account places the loss in warehouses near the harbour rather than the Library itself. Strabo visited decades later and describes the institution still functioning.

Did the Caliph Omar destroy the Library?

Almost certainly not. That story first appears in sources written around six hundred years after the supposed event, and the Library had effectively ceased to exist long before the Arab conquest of Egypt in 642 CE.

Was Hypatia the last librarian of Alexandria?

No. Hypatia was a mathematician and Neoplatonist philosopher murdered by a mob in 415 CE. Her death was a real atrocity, but she held no position at the Library, which had ceased functioning as an institution well before her lifetime.

How many books did the Library hold?

Unknown. Ancient figures range from 40,000 to 700,000 and are unreliable. They also count scrolls, not works — a single long text could occupy many scrolls, so the totals overstate the number of distinct books considerably.

Sources & further reading

  • Roger S. Bagnall, ‘Alexandria: Library of Dreams’, Proceedings of the American Philosophical Society 146 (2002) — the essential corrective.
  • Cassius Dio, Roman History 42.38 — the fire of 48 BCE, and what it actually reached.
  • Strabo, Geography 17.1.8 — an eyewitness describing the Mouseion decades after Caesar.
  • Ammianus Marcellinus 22.16 — a fourth-century writer referring to the library in the past tense.
  • Diana Delia, ‘From Romance to Rhetoric: The Alexandrian Library in Classical and Islamic Traditions’, AHR 97 (1992).

In north-western Greece, near the village of Mesopotamos, three rivers converge in a low marshy basin that was, in antiquity, a lake. The rivers are the Acheron, the Kokytos and the Pyriphlegethon — the rivers of the dead.

These are not names later scholars imposed on the landscape. In the Odyssey, Circe tells Odysseus how to reach the entrance to the house of Hades, and she describes exactly this: a place where Pyriphlegethon and Kokytos flow into Acheron, near a grove of Persephone. Herodotus records that the tyrant Periander of Corinth sent men to an oracle of the dead on the Acheron to question his dead wife.

On a rocky hill above the old lakebed stand the substantial remains of a Hellenistic building. Since 1958 it has been known as the Necromanteion — the Oracle of the Dead. It is signposted, ticketed, and reproduced in a great many books.

The identification is probably wrong, and how it came to be so widely accepted is a case study worth understanding.

Dakaris's reconstruction

Sotirios Dakaris excavated the site over several seasons and produced an account of extraordinary vividness. It runs approximately as follows.

A pilgrim seeking to consult the dead arrived and was admitted to the complex. They were confined for an extended period — days, perhaps weeks — in dark chambers, isolated, on a controlled diet including broad beans, pork and shellfish. Dakaris suggested this regime had psychoactive effects, aided by darkness and sensory deprivation.

They then progressed through a deliberately disorienting sequence: corridors turning at right angles, a labyrinth, purifications at each threshold, offerings, and stone gateways. Finally they descended into a vaulted subterranean chamber cut beneath the central hall, where the encounter took place.

And there, Dakaris proposed, the priests produced the apparition. He had recovered bronze fragments including toothed wheels, which he interpreted as parts of a windlass or crane — machinery to raise a figure or an image into view above the disoriented, half-starved, terrified pilgrim.

It is a magnificent reconstruction. It has everything: sensory deprivation, pharmacology, sacred architecture, and priestly stagecraft. It reads like the climax of a novel, and it entered popular literature immediately and permanently.

Why specialists no longer accept it

The objections accumulated over the following decades and are now, collectively, close to decisive.

The machinery is a weapon. Dietrich Baatz examined the bronze fragments and identified them as components of a torsion catapult — a well-known Hellenistic artillery type with a substantial comparative literature. The toothed wheel is a ratchet from the loading mechanism. Once that identification is accepted, the crane vanishes, and with it the staged apparition.

The finds are agricultural. The site produced large storage jars, quantities of grain, iron tools, and the general assemblage of an estate that stored and processed food. Beans, invoked as a hallucinogen in the reconstruction, are a staple crop. They are what you would expect in a pantry.

The architecture is defensive. The walls are thick polygonal masonry of a kind used for fortification. The complex sits on a defensible height. The layout compares closely to other fortified rural residences known from Hellenistic Epirus — a type of building that exists in quantity and is well understood.

The “underground chamber” is a basement. The vaulted space beneath the central hall is a substantial cellar with barrel vaulting. Storage cellars of this kind are common. Nothing about it requires a chthonic explanation.

The destruction date fits the wrong story. The complex was destroyed in the mid-second century BCE, consistent with the Roman devastation of Epirus in 167 BCE, when Aemilius Paullus reportedly sacked seventy settlements. That is a military event affecting military and domestic sites.

Assemble these and the building resolves into something ordinary: a fortified farmhouse with a cellar, artillery for defence, and a large granary — destroyed, like much of Epirus, by Rome.

How this happens

Dakaris was not a fraud. He was excavating in a landscape that ancient literature explicitly identifies as the entrance to the underworld, and he found an unusual building with a strange sunken chamber. The interpretive leap is understandable. What made it stick was that it was a better story than the alternative, and better stories propagate faster than corrections. The site's signage and the tourist literature still largely reflect the 1958 reading.

What survives the correction

Losing the building does not lose the practice, and it is important to be clear about that.

Greek necromancy is well attested independently. Herodotus's account of Periander is a serious piece of evidence for an oracle of the dead operating somewhere in this region in the archaic period. Several other nekyomanteia are named in ancient sources: at Cape Tainaron in the southern Peloponnese, at Herakleia Pontike on the Black Sea, at Lake Avernus in Campania.

The practice appears across the ancient world in forms ranging from state-sanctioned consultation to the freelance rituals preserved in the magical papyri, where operators summon the dead directly. Meanwhile curse tablets were routinely deposited in graves on the explicit assumption that the dead could receive messages and act on them. An entire population believed the dead were reachable, and behaved accordingly.

So: the oracle on the Acheron very probably existed. We simply do not know where it was. It may lie under the marsh, or under the modern village, or it may have been an arrangement of grove, shore and ritual that left no architecture to find.

Why this site belongs here

This blog is mostly about knowledge that was deliberately withheld. Ephyra is the inverse problem, and a necessary corrective.

Nobody hid anything at Mesopotamos. The site was excavated professionally, published, and remains open. What went wrong is that a reconstruction with the right emotional shape — darkness, drugs, machinery, priests deceiving the desperate — escaped the evidence supporting it, and could not be recalled once it was loose.

The ancient world is unusually vulnerable to this. It is distant, the evidence is thin, and the gaps are large enough to hold almost any story you care to put in them. The discipline that makes the genuine mysteries worth reading about — asking what the evidence actually supports, and stopping there — is the same discipline that dissolves this one.

The building on the hill is almost certainly a farm. The oracle of the dead is still out there somewhere, unlocated, in a valley that Homer thought was the doorway to the underworld. That is a better ending than the machinery.

Questions people actually ask

What is the Necromanteion of Acheron?

A Hellenistic building complex at Mesopotamos in Epirus, north-western Greece, excavated from 1958 and identified by its excavator as a nekyomanteion — an oracle where the living consulted the dead.

Was there really an oracle of the dead in this region?

Almost certainly yes. Herodotus records Periander of Corinth sending envoys to an oracle of the dead on the Acheron, and the river landscape matches Homer's description of the entrance to the underworld. The literary evidence is solid; the identification of this particular building is not.

Why do archaeologists doubt the identification?

The finds fit a fortified rural estate: storage jars, grain, agricultural tools, thick defensive walls. The bronze fragments interpreted as apparition machinery have been convincingly reidentified as parts of a torsion catapult.

Were pilgrims given hallucinogenic drugs there?

That was proposed on the basis of beans and other foodstuffs recovered at the site, but the pharmacological argument was never strong and the underlying identification of the building is now in doubt. There is no reliable evidence for it.

What is a nekyomanteion?

A Greek oracle where the dead, rather than a god, were consulted. Several are attested in ancient literature — on the Acheron, at Cape Tainaron, at Herakleia Pontike, and at Lake Avernus in Italy.

Sources & further reading

  • Sotirios Dakaris, The Nekyomanteion of the Acheron (Athens, 1993) — the excavator's own account and reconstruction.
  • Dietrich Baatz, ‘Hellenistische Katapulte aus Ephyra’, Athenische Mitteilungen 97 (1982) — the reidentification of the bronze fragments.
  • Daniel Ogden, Greek and Roman Necromancy (Princeton, 2001) — the standard treatment, and sceptical of the site.
  • Herodotus, Histories 5.92 — Periander and the oracle of the dead.
  • Homer, Odyssey 10.508–515 and Book 11 — Circe's directions, and the topography of the underworld's entrance.

item.title: The Piacenza Liver: A Map of the Sky Drawn on an Organ
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
In 1877, a farmer ploughing a field near Settima, not far from Piacenza in northern Italy, turned up a piece of bronze about the size of a hand. It is shaped like a sheep's liver, complete with the lobes and the protruding processus pyramidalis, modelled accurately enough that a veterinarian would recognise the organ.

The flat underside is divided by incised lines into forty compartments — sixteen running around the perimeter, twenty-four arranged within. Each compartment carries an inscription: the abbreviated name of a god.

It is not decoration and it is not a votive offering. It is a piece of professional equipment, and it is the closest thing we have to a surviving instrument from a religious technology that the Roman state relied on for eight hundred years.

Reading the future in an animal

The Etruscans practised haruspicy — divination by inspecting the entrails of a sacrificed animal, with particular attention to the liver.

The choice is less arbitrary than it sounds. The liver is large, densely vascularised, and highly variable between individuals. It shows disease clearly, changes colour and texture readily, and presents an abundance of features to interpret: lobes, fissures, the gall bladder, marks and swellings. If you require a natural object with enough detail to yield a specific reading every time, it is a good choice. Mesopotamian diviners had reached the same conclusion centuries earlier, and clay liver models survive from Babylonia too.

The Etruscan system worked by correspondence. The liver was treated as a small-scale model of the cosmos. The sky was divided into regions, each belonging to a deity, and those regions were mapped onto the surface of the organ. A mark appearing in a given zone was therefore a communication from the god who owned the matching quarter of heaven — and its position told you both who was speaking and whether the message was favourable.

The bronze liver is the key to that mapping. It is a reference model: a physical lookup table, showing which god belongs where.

The sixteen regions, corroborated

The most important feature is the ring of sixteen divisions around the edge, because this is where the object connects to independent evidence.

Roman writers record that Etruscan doctrine divided the sky into sixteen parts for the interpretation of lightning — a system in which the direction from which a bolt came determined which god had sent it and what it meant. Pliny the Elder describes the scheme. Martianus Capella, writing much later, provides a list of the deities inhabiting the sixteen celestial regions.

The perimeter of the Piacenza Liver has sixteen divisions, and the names inscribed in them correspond, where they can be read, to the pattern those Roman sources describe.

That correspondence does two things. It confirms that Roman accounts of Etruscan religion were reporting a real system rather than inventing an exotic one. And it confirms what the object is for: the liver in the diviner's hands was a small copy of the sky above him, and reading one was reading the other.

The orientation problem

Note what this requires in practice. The haruspex had to hold the organ in a specific orientation relative to the actual compass directions, so that the zones aligned with the correct quarters of the real sky. Get the orientation wrong and every reading inverts. This is a skill with a correct and incorrect execution — which is exactly why a training model in durable bronze would be worth commissioning.

The books that Rome quoted and nobody kept

Behind the instrument stood a literature. The Romans called it the Etrusca disciplina, and described it as transmitted in three groups of books:

  • The libri haruspicini, on reading entrails.
  • The libri fulgurales, on lightning — its regions, its meanings, and the rituals for handling a struck place.
  • The libri rituales, on ritual law: how to found a city, lay out boundaries, consecrate temples, and how long the ages of the world would last.

That third category deserves emphasis. Roman city-founding ritual — the sacred boundary, the orientation, the plough drawn around the perimeter — was understood by Romans themselves to derive from Etruscan practice. This was not a fringe superstition Rome tolerated. It was structural.

Rome took it seriously enough to institutionalise it. There was an official order of haruspices. Etruscan noble families supplied practitioners, and young Romans were sent to learn the discipline. Haruspices were consulted by the Senate, attached to emperors, and still operating in the fourth century CE. In 408 CE, with Alaric outside the walls, haruspices are reported to have offered to call down lightning on the Gothic army.

Not one of those books survives. We possess quotations, summaries, and hostile paraphrases in Latin authors — Cicero, Seneca, Pliny, Macrobius, Ammianus — and nothing else.

The second lock on the door

Even the fragments that survive in Etruscan are only partly legible, and the reason is unusual.

The alphabet is not the problem. Etruscan was written in a script derived from Greek, and it can be transliterated with confidence — we know how the words sounded. The problem is the language itself. Etruscan is not Indo-European. It has no securely established relatives beyond the fragmentary Lemnian and Raetic, which are too poorly attested to help much.

So there is no cognate vocabulary to work from. Meaning has to be extracted from context, from bilingual inscriptions where they exist, and from repetition — and the surviving corpus of roughly thirteen thousand inscriptions is dominated by short funerary formulae. Names, ages, family relationships, offices. Enormously useful for grammar and titles; almost useless for theology.

The longest surviving Etruscan text reached us by a route that is difficult to improve on for strangeness. A linen book, apparently a ritual calendar of around twelve hundred readable words, was at some point cut into strips and used to wrap an Egyptian mummy. It was acquired in Egypt in the nineteenth century, taken to Croatia, and only later recognised for what it was. It survives because someone in Ptolemaic Egypt needed bandages.

Even so, it can only be partly understood. We can identify it as a calendar of rites, pick out gods and dates and repeated ritual instructions, and follow the structure — without reliably knowing what the ceremonies were for.

The dictionary that would have solved it

There is one loss here that is genuinely painful to contemplate.

The emperor Claudius was a serious scholar with an antiquarian obsession, and his first wife was Etruscan. He wrote a history of the Etruscans in twenty books — the Tyrrhenica — and is reported to have compiled a dictionary of the language. He had access to native speakers, to family archives, and to a priesthood still practising. He had the resources of the Roman state and no shortage of time.

Every word of it is gone.

No fire is required to explain this. Texts survive only where somebody keeps choosing to copy them, and a twenty-book history of a defunct people in a dead language, by an emperor with a poor posthumous reputation, was never going to compete for scribal labour against Virgil.

What we have instead is a piece of bronze from a ploughed field: forty compartments, forty divine names, and a discipline that shaped how Rome founded its cities and read its sky — reduced to a hand-sized object that we can hold, and describe, and not quite read.

Questions people actually ask

What is the Piacenza Liver?

A bronze model of a sheep's liver, about 126 mm long, found near Piacenza in northern Italy in 1877 and dated to roughly 100 BCE. Its surface is divided into forty regions, each inscribed with the abbreviated name of an Etruscan deity.

What was it used for?

Almost certainly as a teaching or reference instrument for haruspicy — divination by reading the liver of a sacrificed animal. The model told the practitioner which god corresponded to which zone of the organ.

What is haruspicy?

The Etruscan practice of interpreting the will of the gods by examining the entrails, especially the liver, of sacrificed animals. Rome adopted it, maintained official haruspices, and consulted them into the fourth century CE.

Can we read Etruscan?

Phonetically, yes — Etruscan uses a Greek-derived alphabet, so the sounds are recoverable. The language itself is only partly understood. It is not Indo-European and has no well-attested close relatives, so most vocabulary must be inferred from context.

What was the Etrusca disciplina?

The Etruscan body of religious lore, transmitted in books covering entrail-reading, lightning interpretation, and ritual law including the founding of cities. Every one of those books is lost; we know them only through Roman quotation and summary.

Sources & further reading

  • Nancy Thomson de Grummond, Etruscan Myth, Sacred History and Legend (2006).
  • Jean MacIntosh Turfa, Divining the Etruscan World: The Brontoscopic Calendar and Religious Practice (2012).
  • Cicero, On Divination — a Roman augur's sceptical but detailed account of the discipline.
  • Pliny the Elder, Natural History 2.143 — the sixteenfold division of the sky in Etruscan lightning doctrine.
  • Martianus Capella, De nuptiis 1.41–61 — a late list of the deities of the sixteen celestial regions.
  • The Liber Linteus Zagrabiensis — the longest surviving Etruscan text, preserved as the wrappings of an Egyptian mummy.
